heuristics.rule: Ask current 3rd-5th year students what they actually earn, not what the offer letter states
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a Canadian PhD funding offer...
heuristics.action: ...contact current advanced PhD students in the lab/department and ask their annual total income directly
heuristics.because: Offer letters often reflect first-year or best-case funding; later years frequently drop when fellowships expire or supervisor grants shrink

heuristics.rule: If any portion of the stipend is contingent on winning external competitions, discount it entirely when assessing baseline livability
heuristics.condition: When a Canadian PhD offer includes OGS, CGRS-D, or Vanier as part of the funding package...
heuristics.action: ...calculate whether the guaranteed floor (excluding competitive awards) covers your cost of living before accepting
heuristics.because: External award competitions are not guaranteed; students who budget assuming they will win and then don't face severe financial stress mid-PhD

heuristics.rule: Apply a CAD-to-USD haircut of ~25-27% when comparing Canadian and US stipends, then add back ~$2,000-$6,000 USD for avoided US health insurance costs
heuristics.condition: When an international student is comparing a Canadian PhD offer to a US PhD offer on dollar amounts...
heuristics.action: ...convert CAD to USD at current exchange rate, then adjust upward by $2,000-$4,000 to account for Canadian universal healthcare savings
heuristics.because: Raw dollar comparisons overstate the US advantage; health insurance is a major hidden cost in the US system that Canada eliminates

heuristics.rule: Treat any PhD offer below CAD $28,000/year in Toronto or Vancouver as financially precarious, not just 'modest'
heuristics.condition: When evaluating stipend adequacy in high cost-of-living Canadian cities...
heuristics.action: ...use $28,000-$32,000 CAD/year as the practical comfort threshold, not the published institutional minimum
heuristics.because: A $24,000 CAD stipend in Toronto equals ~$1,833/month pre-tax, which barely covers rent for a 1BR apartment leaving near-zero margin for all other expenses

heuristics.rule: Treat Montreal and Edmonton as structurally better financial environments for PhD students than Toronto or Vancouver, all else equal
heuristics.condition: When choosing between Canadian universities with similar research fit and stipend levels...
heuristics.action: ...weight cost of living heavily; a $26,000 CAD stipend in Montreal is meaningfully more livable than the same amount in Vancouver or Toronto
heuristics.because: Montreal 1BR rent is $1,300-$1,800/month versus $2,100-$3,000/month in Vancouver — the same dollar amount produces radically different quality of life

heuristics.rule: Ask explicitly what happens to your funding if your supervisor's grant runs out before you finish
heuristics.condition: When finalizing a PhD offer with a specific supervisor...
heuristics.action: ...directly ask the supervisor this question and assess the clarity and confidence of their answer before committing
heuristics.because: Supervisor grant expiry is a common but rarely disclosed risk that can leave students mid-PhD with no funding and no clear resolution path

decision_factors.factor: Guaranteed funding floor vs. total package headline
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The headline package often includes competitive awards that may not materialize; the floor determines actual financial security
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'What is my funding if I win no external competitions?' and get a specific number; compare that floor to local cost of living

decision_factors.factor: Funding duration (all 5 years vs. first 2 years only)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Some Canadian programs guarantee funding only for initial years; students in years 4-6 face funding gaps that force them to over-TA or take on debt
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask specifically: 'Is this funding guaranteed for all 4-5 years or just the first 2?' and request this in writing if possible

decision_factors.factor: City cost of living relative to stipend level
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The same nominal stipend produces radically different financial stress depending on the city; a stipend adequate in Waterloo or Edmonton is precarious in Toronto or Vancouver
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check current 1BR rental prices in the program city; calculate post-tax monthly stipend and compare to monthly rent as a ratio

decision_factors.why_it_matters: STEM PhD stipends in Canada ($22,000-$45,000+) vastly exceed humanities stipends ($17,000-$28,000); the risk of funding gaps in years 5+ is concentrated in non-STEM fields
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the typical stipend range for the specific department and field, not just the university average

decision_factors.why_it_matters: TAships supplement income but consume research time; heavy TAship loads (15+ hours/week) significantly delay thesis completion and extend time-to-degree
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current students how many hours per week TAships actually require vs. stated hours; ask if TAing is mandatory or optional

decision_factors.factor: Supervisor grant stability and funding track record
decision_factors.why_it_matters: In Canada, most non-Tri-Council PhD funding flows through supervisor research grants; a supervisor with expiring or thin grants is a direct financial risk to the student
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the supervisor directly about grant status and renewal timeline; check NSERC/CIHR/SSHRC public databases for recent awards to the supervisor

decision_factors.factor: CAD/USD exchange rate impact for international students
decision_factors.why_it_matters: International students sending remittances home or comparing Canadian offers to US offers must account for the ~25-27% CAD discount against USD
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Convert all Canadian stipend figures to USD at current exchange rate (~0.73-0.75) before comparing to US program offers

decision_factors.factor: Healthcare cost savings vs. US equivalent
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Canadian provincial health coverage eliminates $2,000-$6,000/year in health insurance costs that US PhD students face; this meaningfully adjusts real purchasing power comparisons
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check provincial health plan costs for international students (e.g., Ontario UHIP ~$756/year, BC MSP subsidized); subtract from US health insurance cost to compute benefit

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a Canadian PhD offer based on total package including competitive fellowship components
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If the student fails to win OGS, CGRS-D, or other competitive awards, the actual annual income drops to the institutional minimum, which may be $10,000-$15,000 CAD less than the stated package — potentially below cost-of-living threshold in major cities
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students unfamiliar with Canadian funding structures who treat offer letters as guaranteed income

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a PhD program at UBC or UofT for prestige in high-cost cities
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Stipends at these universities, while nominally higher than lower-ranked Canadian schools, are consumed by rent that can equal or exceed 100% of monthly take-home pay, creating financial stress that directly impairs research quality and mental health
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students from lower-cost countries who underestimate Toronto and Vancouver rent levels

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on TAship income as a stable supplement to base stipend
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: TAship hours requirements are frequently underreported; actual weekly demands during term can reach 15-20 hours, leaving insufficient time for research and silently extending time-to-degree by 1-2 years
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in programs where TAship is mandatory or where the base stipend is too low to live without TA income

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting Canada's 2024 federal stipend increase at face value as a sign of improved PhD financial conditions
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The increases apply only to Tri-Council award holders — a minority of all PhD students. The vast majority funded through supervisor grants see no increase, meaning the headline policy change masks ongoing financial hardship for most
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Prospective PhD students who read news coverage of the 2024 budget announcement and assume all Canadian PhD students will receive $40,000/year

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing humanities or social science PhD programs in Canada
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Funding in years 5+ is frequently not guaranteed; students face a high probability of funding gaps requiring emergency TAing, external employment, or debt — a structural feature of humanities PhD funding in Canada, not an exception
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students in social sciences and humanities who plan to finish in 4-5 years but realistically need 6-7 years

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Comparing Canadian PhD stipends to US stipends using nominal dollar amounts without exchange rate adjustment
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A $40,000 CAD stipend looks competitive against a $35,000 USD US offer, but after exchange rate conversion equals only ~$29,000 USD — meaningfully below the US offer in absolute purchasing power for internationally mobile students
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students making simultaneous decisions between Canadian and US PhD offers

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a PhD offer without asking what the guaranteed funding floor is if no external awards are won
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Offer letters present a total package figure that sounds sufficient; students are excited about admission and don't probe the contingency structure of the funding
failure_patterns.consequence: Student arrives and discovers their base institutional funding is $18,000-$22,000 CAD/year rather than the $35,000+ stated in the offer, creating immediate financial crisis in an expensive city
warning_signs: Offer letter lists multiple funding sources without specifying which are guaranteed vs. competitive
Program mentions 'expected' or 'anticipated' funding rather than 'guaranteed' funding

failure_patterns.pattern: Assuming the 2024 federal stipend increases apply to all Canadian PhD students
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Media coverage of the federal budget announcement was widely circulated; the critical caveat — that increases only apply to Tri-Council award holders — was buried or omitted in most reporting
failure_patterns.consequence: Students choose Canadian programs over US alternatives expecting $40,000/year, then receive $22,000-$26,000 CAD/year base funding with no path to the higher rate without winning competitive awards
warning_signs: Student cites the 2024 federal announcement as a reason Canadian stipends are now competitive without verifying their specific program's actual funding
Student has not asked the specific program what percentage of entering PhD students win CGRS-D

failure_patterns.pattern: Underestimating Vancouver and Toronto rent relative to stipend
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students research stipend levels but use national or home-country cost-of-living intuitions rather than current local rental market data; rent in these cities has risen sharply since pre-pandemic norms
failure_patterns.consequence: Student cannot cover basic living expenses on stipend alone, leading to financial stress, side employment that delays research, or early program departure
warning_signs: Student has not checked current Craigslist or Rentals.ca listings for the specific city
Student's budget assumes rent below $1,500/month in Toronto or Vancouver

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating TAship income as reliable supplemental income rather than a time-cost tradeoff
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students see TA stipends as 'free money' added to base funding without accounting for the 10-20 hours/week of actual labor involved during teaching terms
failure_patterns.consequence: Research progress slows significantly during TA terms; thesis timeline extends; students who TA heavily in years 1-3 often face compressed, low-quality dissertation completion in later years
warning_signs: Student is relying on TAship income to meet basic budget rather than treating it as optional
Student has not asked current PhD students how many hours per week TAships actually require

failure_patterns.pattern: Choosing a Canadian PhD program without asking what happens to funding if the supervisor's grant expires
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Students focus on advisor research fit and reputation; funding continuity feels like an awkward question to ask a potential supervisor during the courtship phase of application
failure_patterns.consequence: Mid-PhD funding loss forces the student to scramble for alternative funding, switch supervisors, or abandon the program entirely — all costly outcomes that disproportionately affect international students with visa tied to enrollment
warning_signs: Supervisor has not proactively mentioned grant renewal timeline or funding guarantee duration
Supervisor's most recent major grant was awarded more than 3-4 years ago with no visible renewal

diagnostic_questions.question: Is any portion of your offered PhD funding contingent on winning an external competition like OGS or CGRS-D?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Distinguishes between guaranteed income and aspirational package; determines real financial floor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What is your guaranteed annual funding if you win zero external awards? Is that amount enough to live on in your program city?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is the full amount guaranteed for all years of the program, or only the first 2-3 years?

diagnostic_questions.question: What city is the program in, and what is the current market rent for a 1BR apartment there?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether the stipend is livable or merely nominal; city choice dramatically affects financial stress regardless of stipend level
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you calculated your post-tax monthly stipend and compared it to current rental listings on Rentals.ca or Craigslist?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If you haven't researched current rents, your budget assumptions may be based on outdated or national average data that understates costs in Toronto and Vancouver

diagnostic_questions.question: What field are you entering — STEM, social sciences, or humanities?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Field is a major predictor of funding level and funding gap risk; humanities students face structurally different financial conditions than STEM students at the same university
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If STEM: Is your supervisor's grant recently renewed or mid-cycle? If humanities: Is funding guaranteed beyond year 3?

diagnostic_questions.question: Are you also considering US PhD programs, and if so, have you adjusted the Canadian stipend for the CAD/USD exchange rate?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the student is making an apples-to-apples comparison or being misled by nominal dollar equivalence
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: After exchange rate conversion, is the Canadian offer still competitive? Have you also added back $2,000-$4,000 for healthcare savings?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not comparing to US programs, this factor is less relevant — but cost of living in Canada still requires city-specific assessment

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the mandatory TAship requirement in your program, and how many hours per week do current students actually spend on TA duties?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Distinguishes between official stated TA hours (often 5-10/week) and actual TA hours (often 12-20/week during term); reveals real research time available
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If TA hours are high: Have you calculated how many research hours per week remain after TA duties, coursework, and administrative time?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If TA is optional: Are you financially dependent on TA income to meet your budget, which would make it functionally mandatory?

diagnostic_questions.question: When was your potential supervisor's most recent major grant funded, and when does it expire?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Identifies the financial risk horizon of the supervisory relationship; a supervisor with a grant expiring in year 2 of a 5-year PhD is a material financial risk
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Has the supervisor explicitly discussed what happens to your funding if the grant is not renewed?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If the supervisor hasn't raised this: Ask directly — a good supervisor will have a clear and reassuring answer; evasiveness is a warning sign

industry_realities.common_belief: Canada's 2024 federal budget raised PhD stipends to $40,000/year, making Canadian programs newly competitive with US programs
industry_realities.actual_reality: The $40,000/year increase applies only to Tri-Council award holders (CGRS-D, Vanier). The vast majority of PhD students funded through supervisor research grants see no increase and continue receiving $22,000-$30,000 CAD/year at most institutions
industry_realities.implication: Prospective students must ask specifically whether their funding comes from Tri-Council awards or supervisor grants before treating the $40,000 figure as relevant to their situation

industry_realities.common_belief: Canadian PhD stipends are lower than US stipends, making Canada a financially inferior option
industry_realities.actual_reality: After adjusting for CAD/USD exchange rate and adding back $2,000-$6,000 in health insurance savings, a $30,000 CAD Canadian stipend is roughly equivalent in real purchasing power to a $22,000-$24,000 USD US stipend with employer-covered insurance
industry_realities.implication: The financial comparison is closer than nominal dollar figures suggest, but still favors US programs at the top end; students should do the adjusted math rather than accepting surface-level comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: The stipend listed in a PhD offer letter is what you will receive throughout your program
industry_realities.actual_reality: Canadian PhD offers frequently include competitive fellowship amounts that are not guaranteed; the baseline institutional guarantee is often $5,000-$15,000 CAD/year less than the headline figure
industry_realities.implication: Students must explicitly ask for the guaranteed funding floor and assess livability on that basis, not the advertised package

industry_realities.common_belief: Major Canadian research universities (UofT, UBC) offer the best financial conditions for PhD students because they have the largest budgets
industry_realities.actual_reality: UofT and UBC are located in Canada's two most expensive cities; their higher nominal stipends are substantially offset by rent that can consume 80-100% of monthly take-home pay. McGill (Montreal) and University of Waterloo often provide better real purchasing power despite lower headline numbers
industry_realities.implication: Ranking programs by nominal stipend without adjusting for city cost of living produces systematically misleading financial comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: TAship income is free money added to research stipend that improves PhD financial conditions
industry_realities.actual_reality: TAships are labor that consumes 10-20 hours per week during term; students who rely on TA income to meet basic expenses are effectively trading research time for survival income, which extends time-to-degree and increases total cost of the PhD
industry_realities.implication: TAship dependency should be treated as a financial red flag about the base stipend level, not a feature of the offer

industry_realities.common_belief: 90% of PhD students at major Canadian universities receive full funding covering tuition and living expenses
industry_realities.actual_reality: A 2023 national survey found nearly 90% of Canadian graduate students reported financial stress, with almost one-third considering leaving academia due to money pressures — indicating that nominal funding coverage does not translate to actual financial adequacy
industry_realities.implication: Coverage of tuition and provision of a stipend does not mean the stipend is livable; students must assess the actual dollar amounts against real cost of living, not just whether funding exists

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to evaluate a PhD funding offer
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Reads the total package figure in the offer letter, confirms it's above a round-number threshold (e.g., 'over $30,000'), and concludes the funding is adequate
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Decomposes the package into guaranteed vs. contingent components, calculates post-tax monthly income, compares to current rental listings in the specific city, and asks current 4th-5th year students what they actually earn
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The headline figure routinely overstates guaranteed income by $5,000-$15,000 CAD/year; juniors make acceptance decisions on misleading numbers while seniors verify the actual floor

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Interpreting policy announcements about stipend increases
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Reads that Canada raised PhD stipends to $40,000/year and updates their mental model of all Canadian PhD funding to reflect this
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Immediately asks 'who does this apply to?' and identifies that the increase applies only to Tri-Council award holders, leaving the majority of PhD students unaffected
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Policy announcements in graduate funding frequently have critical carve-outs that determine whether the change is relevant to any specific student; failing to identify the caveat produces systematically wrong financial expectations

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Comparing Canadian vs. US PhD offers
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares headline dollar amounts directly (e.g., '$35,000 CAD vs. $32,000 USD — Canada is higher!') without exchange rate conversion or healthcare adjustment
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Converts CAD to USD at current exchange rate (~0.73-0.75), then adjusts for healthcare cost differential ($2,000-$6,000 USD savings in Canada), then compares city cost of living for each offer location
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Direct nominal comparisons can reverse the actual financial ranking of offers; seniors make multi-variable adjusted comparisons while juniors use single-variable surface comparisons

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses entirely on supervisor's research reputation, publication record, and personality fit; does not think to ask about grant status or funding continuity
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats supervisor grant status as a material financial risk variable; asks explicitly about grant renewal timelines and what happens to student funding if a grant expires before thesis completion
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Grant expiry mid-PhD is a real and common event in Canadian academia; students who don't assess this risk in advance have no contingency plan when it occurs

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Accounting for city cost of living
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Evaluates funding adequacy using national average cost-of-living intuitions or pre-pandemic rent data; concludes $24,000 CAD is livable because 'Canada is affordable'
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Checks current rental listings on Rentals.ca or Craigslist for the specific city and neighborhood; recognizes that Toronto and Vancouver have among the highest rent-to-income ratios of any academic city in North America
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: City-specific rent variation in Canada is extreme (Edmonton 1BR at $1,200 vs. Vancouver at $2,600); using national averages produces errors large enough to determine whether a student can afford to eat, not just save

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Treating TAship as income vs. labor
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Sees TAship stipend as a straightforward income supplement that makes the financial package better
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Calculates the hourly rate implied by TA stipend vs. actual TA hours, recognizes that TA obligations are a time tax on research, and assesses whether base stipend alone covers living expenses
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Students financially dependent on TAship income cannot say no to TA assignments even when they conflict with critical research milestones, creating a structural incentive that extends time-to-degree
